sections.preamble:
You segment one lesion in a 3D MRI volume by operating an interactive segmentation model (nnInteractive) through `seg_*` tools. You cannot run code or read files; the tools are your only actions. Each tool returns text and, usually, images.

## How pointing works
You never type coordinates. You point with **marks**: numbered labels drawn on the images.
- Integer marks (e.g. `17`) are fixed 3D points spread over the body. Circles mark bright spots, squares mark dark spots, triangles mark centres of uniform regions. The same number refers to the same point in every view.
- Marks starting with `E` (e.g. `E4`) lie on edges in the current image only. Use them as outline vertices.
- All spatial arguments refer to the **current view**: the last image returned by `seg_view`. A mark is valid only if it is drawn in that view. When you use a mark, its position on the current slice is used.
- A full-slice view shows coarse marks only. To get denser marks in a region, call `seg_view` with `crop: "marks"` and `ids` = one or more marks of the current view around that region (it zooms there and shows fine marks), or `crop: "mask"` once a mask exists. Use `marks: "edges"` to get edge marks for outlining.
- Each `seg_view` returns two panels: left is the clean image, right has the marks. Compare them; labels can hide detail.

## Workflow
1. **Find the lesion.** `seg_open` gives the case card and an overview. Scan the volume with `seg_sheet` in at least two planes before choosing. The target is an abnormal mass that displaces or replaces normal tissue; do not mistake normal anatomy (bone and marrow, vessels, bladder, bowel, joints, fat) for it. If both limbs are visible, compare them: the lesion makes one side differ from the other.
2. **Start the mask** with a prompt on the lesion: `seg_view` the slice where it is largest, then a positive `seg_point` on a mark inside it, or `seg_lasso`/`seg_box` around it.
3. **Check and correct.** After every edit you get an image with three planes (axial, coronal, sagittal) through the mask with surrounding tissue. Compare the green outline with the lesion edge in all three planes, especially at the upper and lower ends: one prompt rarely captures a large or heterogeneous lesion. To add a missed part, `seg_view` a slice through it and place positive points (or a positive scribble/lasso) there; to remove a leak, place negative points or a negative scribble on it. `seg_paint` edits the mask directly without the model; `seg_refine` lets the model clean up a painted mask. `seg_edit` does component and morphology edits. `seg_undo`/`seg_checkout` restore earlier versions. `seg_candidates` lists automatic proposals of possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong, so judge each by the tissue inside its outline. `seg_accept` adds the chosen candidates to the mask directly (a direct edit, not the model); `seg_refine` can let the model smooth the result afterwards.
4. **Finish** when the outline follows the lesion boundary in all three planes: `seg_finish` with your confidence and a short reason. The first `seg_finish` shows a final review (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent + one just past each end); inspect every panel, fix what is wrong, and call `seg_finish` again with the review code it prints to save. The review also shows candidate corrections in a second image: for each, decide whether the tissue inside its outline is part of the same lesion (accept with `seg_accept`, then finish again for a new review) or normal tissue (reject by not accepting it).

Every edit returns: version id, volume, number of connected components, slice extent per plane, the change from the previous version, budget used, and the three-plane image (green = mask, red = removed).

## Rules
- **What counts as the lesion.** Outline the whole mass the way a radiologist annotating the full tumor would: include its less intense or heterogeneous periphery, the rim or capsule around a bright core, and any extension contiguous with the mass (along fascia, a nerve, or between muscles), over its full length.
- Segment the whole lesion described in the task, and nothing else. If it is multifocal, include all parts.
- Budgets: at most 40 tool calls and 15 model prompts (point/lasso/scribble/box/refine). Every call counts, including views and calls that fail. When the tool-call budget is used up, only `seg_finish` works. Use the budget to check and correct; stop when the mask is good, not after the first result.
- Keep working until you call `seg_finish`. Do not stop to ask questions; nobody will answer.
- Confidence in `seg_finish`: `high` only if the boundary is clearly correct in all three planes; `low` if you are unsure the mask covers the right structure.

toolsAdded.name: seg_accept
toolsAdded.description: Add the chosen candidates from the latest seg_candidates (or final review) to the mask as one new version. A direct edit without the model (seg_refine can smooth it afterwards). Only accept candidates whose tissue is part of the lesion. Fails if the mask changed since the candidates were shown: call seg_candidates again. Counts as a tool call, not a model prompt.

toolsAdded.name: seg_box
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a 2D box. Provide exactly two mark ids on the current slice: the box corners (opposite corners of the bounding rectangle).

ids.description: Exactly two mark ids: the box corners.

toolsAdded.name: seg_candidates
toolsAdded.description: List automatic proposals (C1, C2, ...) of lesion tissue the current mask may have missed, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong. Returns a text list (volume, where each touches the mask) and one image: a row per candidate with axial, coronal and sagittal slices through it, the current mask as a green outline and the candidate as a magenta outline with a light tint. Look at the tissue inside each magenta outline and judge it; nothing changes until you call seg_accept. Candidates belong to the current mask version; any mask change invalidates them. Counts as a tool call.

toolsAdded.name: seg_checkout
toolsAdded.description: Restore a specific mask version id reported in earlier observations (e.g. v3).

toolsAdded.name: seg_edit
toolsAdded.description: Non-model mask edit. keep_component/remove_component need a mark id inside the component. fill_holes/close/open/dilate/erode operate on the whole mask; radius_mm sets the morphology radius (default 2).

toolsAdded.name: seg_finish
toolsAdded.description: Save the final mask and end the case. The first call (without review_code) shows a final review of the current mask (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent and one just past each end), a second image with candidate corrections (possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask: accept those that belong with seg_accept, then review again) and a review code. Check it, fix problems, then call seg_finish again with that review_code to save. Editing after the review requires a new review.

review_code.description: Code printed in the latest final review; required to save.

toolsAdded.name: seg_lasso
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a lasso: at least 3 ordered mark ids on the current slice form a closed polygon around (positive) or inside (negative) the lesion. Prefer this over many points for a rough outline.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_open
toolsAdded.description: Read the case card (volume shape, spacing, sequence, target text, mark convention, budgets) and get an orthogonal overview with orientation letters and a 10 mm scale bar. Call this first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_paint
toolsAdded.description: Edit the mask directly without the model: rasterize the polygon through ordered mark ids on the current slice and apply it to the slice range. mode add fills, mode erase removes. Use seg_refine afterwards to let the model clean the painted boundary.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

slice_range.description: Two slice indices [start, stop] on the current axis, both inclusive.

toolsAdded.name: seg_point
toolsAdded.description: Run the segmentation model from point prompt(s) on the current view. Positive marks seed the lesion; negative marks remove the region under them. Adds to the current mask.

ids.description: Mark ids shown in the current seg_view, in order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_refine
toolsAdded.description: Send the current mask to the model as an initial segmentation so it refines the boundary. Use after seg_paint or a rough lasso.

toolsAdded.name: seg_scribble
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a scribble: ordered mark ids on the current slice form a polyline. Use positive to add a missed region and negative to erase a leak along a line.

ids.description: At least 2 mark ids on the current slice, listed in the order the line should run; the polyline connects them in this order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_sheet
toolsAdded.description: Contact sheet of evenly spaced slices along one axis, each labelled with its slice index. Use it to locate the lesion, then inspect single slices with seg_view.

toolsAdded.name: seg_undo
toolsAdded.description: Restore the parent of the current mask version.

toolsAdded.name: seg_view
toolsAdded.description: Show one slice as a clean panel and a marked panel. Clean + marked are returned side by side. All mark ids refer to the view returned last. crop:'marks' zooms on the given mark ids (from the current view) plus a margin and reveals fine marks there; crop:'mask' zooms on the current mask; marks:'edges' gives edge marks for outlining.

ids.description: Required with crop:'marks': mark ids (int or "E<n>") shown in the current view to zoom on.

content.text:
Case V64: segment the vascular soft-tissue tumor on this T2-weighted MRI.

Volume: 376x376x146 voxels, 1 mm isotropic. Budgets: max 40 tool calls / 15 model prompts / 10 min wall time.
Start with `seg_open`. Finish with `seg_finish`.

case V64 | sequence T2 | shape (i,j,k)=(376, 376, 146) | spacing 1x1x1 mm
target: vascular soft-tissue tumor
display: radiological. axial: patient right LEFT, anterior TOP. coronal: patient right LEFT, superior TOP. sagittal: anterior LEFT, superior TOP. R/L cannot be verified for single limbs.
pointing: set-of-marks only. Global marks are integer IDs (3D); edge marks are 'E<n>' valid only in the current view. Spatial arguments resolve against the last seg_view; call seg_view before pointing. Slice indices are navigation.
lasso/scribble/paint: list mark IDs IN ORDER around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); an out-of-order list self-intersects and fills with holes.
budgets: 40 tool calls, 15 model prompts (exhausted -> call seg_finish).
axial 73/146 | crop full | marks none | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 1/40, prompts 0/15

I'm trying to orient this scan — it looks like a chest MRI with lungs visible bilaterally around slices 105-145, though I'm uncertain whether this is truly axial or another plane given the odd anatomy alignment, and I'm puzzling over what the bright round structure near the spine represents.

Looking more carefully at the slices, I'm now wondering if this could instead be a limb cross-section (thigh or arm) rather than chest, since some slices show a round bone-like structure with a bright rim rather than paired lungs — the various bright spots at different coordinates across slices might be vascular flow signals from the tumor. I should check the sagittal view and individual slices to clarify the actual anatomy before going further.

content.thinking:
I'm realizing the axes are permuted: the displayed "sagittal" plane actually shows the real axial chest view with both lungs, while the labeled "axial" view is really a coronal slice. So the true patient axial orientation corresponds to what's displayed as sagittal.

I'm trying to locate the tumor by tracking bright round structures across slices - candidates like the aorta or a vessel appear consistently in similar positions across several slices, but the axis confusion makes it hard to pin down whether these correspond to a vascular structure or the spinal canal. I need to look at larger views to resolve this properly.

content.text: axial 132/146 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 5/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
I'm looking at this chest view showing a bright vascular mass with two lobes near the body wall, with septations visible near the body surface—trying to determine if this represents a single tumor along the patient's lateral/posterior chest wall appearing at two points in the slice.

Tracing through other axial levels, the lobulated bright T2 signal with serpentine flow-void-like structures points toward a vascular tumor such as a hemangioma or vascular malformation, with the two lobes likely connected around a constriction point. I'm also checking a separate round bright structure with a gray rim near the midline, which could be the vertebral body, aorta, or a fluid-filled paraspinal structure, trying to pin down its identity across the different slices.

Reconsidering the overall orientation, I realize the two large dark regions represent lungs split by the mediastinum, meaning the vertical axis is actually patient left-right, while the horizontal axis runs posterior to anterior. That reframes the body bulge on one side as the anterior chest wall, suggesting the bilateral bright masses are breast tissue rather than something more unusual.

I'm trying to work out the orientation of this chest acquisition — likely axial slices with posterior on the left, patient right-left running vertically, and slice direction being superior-inferior. I'm now scanning for the vascular tumor, wondering if the large lobulated bright structure near the right edge at axial slice 145 actually represents breast tissue rather than something pathological.

Looking at other slices, I keep spotting bright round structures scattered at various coordinates (axial 40, 53, 105-145), trying to measure their true size using the sheet-to-voxel scale factor. One candidate comes out around 48mm with a gray halo and bright core, which seems too large to be the spinal canal, so I'm reconsidering what anatomical structure this could actually be.

Actually, re-examining the sagittal display orientation, those slices showing paired lungs with the spine below suggest the k-axis actually represents anterior-posterior depth, meaning the 146 slices span the AP extent of the chest rather than a different axis — likely a cropped region rather than the full chest depth.

That would make k low = posterior = bottom, matching the bright round object seen across axial slices 40-145 that stays roughly at the same position, suggesting a tube-like structure running 100+ mm along the AP direction with a width of 40-50mm. That's an odd finding for normal anatomy, so I wonder if I've misread which axis k corresponds to—maybe it's actually the S direction instead.

Actually, the round cross-section staying consistent across slices makes more sense as the spinal canal, which runs craniocaudal—meaning k is actually the S-I axis, and the axial display is a true axial view. That would explain the rotated orientation: spine on the image's left, sternum/breast bulge on the right, two lungs flanking a vertical axis—this is a 90°-rotated axial view with k representing superior-inferior.

Looking at the 146mm FOV covering the chest, the coronal and sagittal sheets now make more sense too: the coronal (i,k) plane shows body width in the AP direction rotated, while the sagittal (j,k) plane—since j is patient R-L—is actually displaying a coronal slice showing both lungs with the mediastinum centered and spine-related structures at the bottom, consistent with the shorter 146mm height of those sheet cells.

Now I'm puzzled by the bright round structure at (265,388) persisting from k=40 to 145, a 45mm vertical tube with bright T2 signal and a gray wall near the posterior mediastinum next to the spine—too large for the descending aorta (~25-30mm) but the gray halo's position anterior toward the heart doesn't fit a simple vertebral body or spinal canal explanation either.

Rechecking my scale, the displayed panel is roughly 768px for 376 voxels (about 2x), so the bright round structure is actually closer to 16mm across, which fits better as the spinal canal with CSF and the gray halo as the cord or vertebral body. That leaves the bulging bright lobulated mass on the right side of the chest, which given a supine patient position looks more like breast tissue.

Reconsidering the orientation, if the spine is at the left edge, then the right side showing two lobes with a central constriction at the sternum line is consistent with normal breast tissue (fibroglandular tissue appearing intermediate-bright against dark fat on T2 fat-sat). So I'm still trying to locate a vascular tumor elsewhere in the chest wall, scanning other bright curved structures in axial slice 40.

Looking at the lower slices, the round object with a bright rim near k=0 and k=13 could actually be an arm or the neck rather than chest, while k=145 clearly shows large lungs with chest wall muscles. I'm trying to figure out exactly where along the body these slices correspond.

The bright soft tissue irregularities around k=40-66 catch my attention, particularly elongated bright structures near the anterior chest wall at axial 66, which could be related to breast tissue or possibly the tumor I'm looking for.

content.text: axial 60/146 | crop full | marks none | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 6/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
This anatomy looks unusual — the slices below k<60 seem to show a different body region, possibly a pelvis or hip area rather than what I'd expect, with an odd field of view that only partially captures the body. I'm noticing small dark round structures that could be lung-like, but the overall shape discontinuity is puzzling me.

I'm wondering if this could be a child or infant body with an unfamiliar orientation, and I'm not confident in resolving it from the current views. I should look more closely at the sagittal and coronal slices around the center index to get better bearings, maybe viewing a denser range to pick out distinguishing features.

content.text: sagittal 227/376 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 7/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
I'm picturing this as a coronal-like view with lungs forming two domes at top and the diaphragm/abdomen below, so slice index k increases going superiorly. At the top slice, I'm trying to identify that bright central blob—possibly the trachea or great vessels in the mediastinum—against the darker lung fields.

Given the task is a "vascular soft-tissue tumor," I'm weighing candidates: the bright lobulated bilateral masses in the anterior chest wall, which look like they could just be breast tissue (fibroglandular tissue appearing bright against darker fat on T2-FS) rather than pathology. I'm also considering the symmetric elongated bright structures near the anterior surface at lower slices, which again seem consistent with normal breast anatomy rather than a true lesion.

I'm second-guessing the anatomy entirely now, wondering if this could actually be a prone breast MRI dataset where the breasts hang dependently, which would explain the symmetric bilateral bright structures better than a chest-wall tumor interpretation.

Both breasts show similarly heterogeneous bright tissue with dark fat, which makes me reconsider whether this is really breast tissue at all—maybe it's some general soft-tissue tumor dataset with an auto-generated label like "hemangioma," and perhaps I'm actually looking at a limb or paired limbs rather than a chest. But the branching bright lines through the dark oval structures really do look like pulmonary vasculature, so I'm leaning back toward this being the chest and lungs.

I'm now tracking several bright round structures across slices to see if they form a consistent anatomical path. One candidate near the posterior region appears at slightly shifting positions across axial levels 40-53, roughly consistent with the spinal canal, while another bright focus holds a stable left-right position from slice 105 through 132, suggesting it's a continuous structure like a vessel rather than noise.

At k=40 there's another bright round mass, roughly 40mm, posterior to the chest wall near the spine — this could be the vascular tumor I'm trying to locate, distinct from the spinal canal itself. I'm cross-checking the spinal canal position across multiple slices to make sure I'm not confusing it with this paraspinal mass.

I should just pull up the full axial 45 and 53 slices directly to get clearer coordinates instead of estimating from the panel crops.

This lesion appears consistently across slices k=40 and k=53, so I want to cross-reference it on the coronal and sagittal views to better characterize its location. I'll place a seg_point marker at this spot to track it.

content.text: Final review of v1: volume 9.3 mL | components 1 (largest 100.0%) | extent axial 33–59, coronal 127–154, sagittal 238–263 | tool calls 16/40, prompts 1/15. The image shows five slices per plane (three inside the mask extent + one just past each end; past-the-mask panels are orange). Check: (1) Is lesion tissue visible in the past-the-mask panels (orange)? Then the mask stops too early: seg_view that slice and add positive points on the lesion there. (2) Does the outline cut through lesion or include normal tissue on any panel? (3) Stray components? If any answer shows a problem, fix it before finishing. Candidates: none found. If everything is right, call seg_finish again with review_code "5422" to save it.

content.text: case V64 finished (confidence medium); final mask saved from v1 | final volume 9.3 mL, components 1 (largest 100.0%) | tool calls 17/40, prompts 1/15
Case finished. The final mask has been saved; do not call any more tools.

I segmented one well-circumscribed, T2-bright round mass of about 9.3 mL (roughly 27 mm across) and saved it. I'm only medium-confident that it is the intended tumor.

- **Why this lesion:** its bright signal and sharp border fit a vascular tumor. The other bright structures I checked looked like normal anatomy: the spinal canal and the breast tissue at the anterior chest wall. I did not identify any other candidate.
- **How I got there:** a single positive point on the mass gave the mask, with no further model edits. The automatic candidate search found nothing missed next to it.
- **Boundary checks:** the outline follows the lesion edge in the axial, coronal and sagittal views. The final review showed no lesion tissue just past either end, and there is one connected component.
- **Weaker spot:** the lower end, around axial slices 33–40, is faint. There the mask covers the bright core and may stop slightly short of a fainter halo.
